title: Polyhedrality of linear-rank inequality cones
formal: For every integer \(n\ge6\), is the cone \(L_n\) of linear rank inequalities valid over every commutative field polyhedral? Equivalently, for each fixed \(n\ge6\), do finitely many valid coefficient vectors generate every universally valid homogeneous linear inequality on the dimensions of all nonempty sums of \(n\) subspaces by nonnegative real linear combination? The finite generating family may depend on \(n\); no common bound on its size as \(n\) varies is assumed.
why: Dimensions of subspace sums describe the information profiles available to linear coding and linear secret-sharing systems. Finite generation would give a finite complete system of universal linear constraints for each fixed number of subspaces. Nonpolyhedrality would show an intrinsic need for infinitely many constraints even after that number is fixed.
status_note: Open in the checked 2022 seminar Problem (4.4). The complete five-variable result does not extend to all n>=6, and the checked scope of later 2025 work on rank inequalities does not settle polyhedrality. Bounded later checks through 2026-09-16 verified no resolution.

progress.text: Dougherty–Freiling–Zeger arXiv v3 gives the complete five-variable description and an incomplete collection of six-variable inequalities.

sentences: Linear rank inequalities constrain the dimensions of every nonempty sum in a collection of subspaces.
The target cone contains the coefficient vectors of inequalities valid over every commutative field.
The question asks whether this cone is polyhedral for each fixed number of subspaces at least six.
A finite description is known through five subspaces, while increasing families of inequalities for larger collections do not themselves settle the fixed-dimension question.
A resolution would determine whether linear information profiles admit a finite complete set of universal linear constraints at each fixed arity.

definitions:
Write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and \(\mathcal S_n=\{S\subseteq[n]:S\ne\varnothing\}\). A subspace arrangement consists of a commutative field \(F\), a nonnegative integer \(m\), and subspaces \(V_1,\ldots,V_n\) of \(F^m\). Finite and infinite fields, every characteristic, arbitrary ambient dimension, repeated subspaces and the zero subspace are all allowed. Its rank vector \(r\in\mathbb R^{\mathcal S_n}\) has coordinate \(r_S=\dim_F(\sum_{i\in S}V_i)\), where the sum denotes the linear span of the listed subspaces and each finite dimension is embedded in \(\mathbb R\).

A real vector \(a=(a_S)_{S\in\mathcal S_n}\) is a universally valid linear rank inequality if \(\sum_{S\in\mathcal S_n}a_Sr_S\ge0\) for every such arrangement, including every choice of \(F\). Define \(L_n\) to be the set of all these coefficient vectors. All inequalities are homogeneous and non-strict; no additive constant, normalization, integrality constraint on coefficients or restriction to a fixed characteristic is included. The empty-set coordinate is omitted because its dimension is always zero. In particular \(L_n\) is a closed convex cone in the finite-dimensional real vector space \(\mathbb R^{2^n-1}\).

Here a cone is polyhedral if it is the intersection of finitely many closed homogeneous real halfspaces. For \(L_n\), this is equivalent to finite generation: there exist a nonnegative integer \(M_n\) and vectors \(a^{(1)},\ldots,a^{(M_n)}\in L_n\) such that
\[
L_n=\left\{\sum_{j=1}^{M_n}\lambda_j a^{(j)}:\lambda_j\in\mathbb R,\ \lambda_j\ge0\right\}.
\]
The empty sum is zero. These generators may have arbitrary real coordinates. No effective procedure for finding them, rationality of a generating family or computational bound is requested.

For clarity, the coefficient cone \(L_n\) is the dual of the closed conic hull \(C_n\) of all rank vectors: \(C_n\) is the Euclidean closure of the set of all finite nonnegative real combinations of arrangement vectors, allowing different fields for different arrangements. Then \(L_n=\{a:\langle a,x\rangle\ge0\ \text{for all }x\in C_n\}\). Polyhedrality of \(C_n\) and \(L_n\) is equivalent. The question does not assert that every point of \(C_n\) is itself the rank vector of one arrangement, or that the unclosed conic hull is already closed.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof that \(L_n\) is polyhedral for every integer \(n\ge6\), or a complete Lean proof that \(L_n\) is not polyhedral for at least one fixed integer \(n\ge6\). A positive answer may establish the existence of finite generating families without an efficient construction. A growing number of required inequalities as \(n\) increases does not by itself refute polyhedrality at any fixed \(n\). Neither a result for unrestricted entropy inequalities nor a result confined to one field characteristic settles the stated all-fields target by itself.

context_blocks.text: Problem (4.4), attributed to Alexander Shen in the 2022 seminar report, asks about the inequality cones for \(n\ge6\). This card uses the field-independent convention for linear rank inequalities from the subspace-arrangement literature. The report separately asks about field-size and characteristic dependence in Problem (8.3); those restricted cones are not silently substituted for \(L_n\).

The coefficient cone of valid inequalities and the closed cone of admissible rank profiles are dual objects. Making the closure and dual convention explicit prevents a claim about a discrete set of integer rank vectors from being mistaken for the polyhedrality question.

Dougherty, Freiling and Zeger give a complete finite set of inequalities on five variables, including 24 additional types beyond the Shannon and Ingleton inequalities. Their six-variable discussion gives further inequalities without a complete finite description.

Later work studies additional rank inequalities and distinctions between representability and common-information conditions, including in the broader setting of skew fields. Such results about individual inequalities or proof methods do not alone determine whether the full all-fields cone is polyhedral.
